reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: A group of inherited retinal dystrophies in which rod photoreceptors degenerate first, so patients present with night blindness (nyctalopia) and progressive peripheral field loss
Field constriction advances to tunnel vision, with central acuity typically preserved until late unless the macula becomes involved
The classic fundus triad is bone-spicule pigmentation in the mid-periphery, waxy pallor of the optic disc, and attenuated retinal arterioles
It may be isolated or part of a syndrome, notably Usher syndrome (with sensorineural deafness) and Bardet-Biedl syndrome, so associated systemic features should be sought
Inheritance can be autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked, which influences prognosis and genetic counselling
Common complications include posterior subcapsular cataract and cystoid macular oedema, both of which are treatable and can improve residual vision
Management focuses on genetic counselling, low-vision support, monitoring for treatable complications, and emerging gene-based therapies for specific mutations
reference.pathophysiology: Retinitis pigmentosa comprises inherited dystrophies caused by mutations in numerous genes essential to photoreceptor and retinal pigment epithelium function. Progressive apoptosis of rod photoreceptors, followed later by cones, leads to loss of peripheral and night vision that spreads centrally over time. Degenerating photoreceptors and migration of retinal pigment epithelial cells into the retina produce the characteristic bone-spicule pigmentation, while secondary changes cause arteriolar narrowing and optic disc pallor. The underlying genetic defect determines the pattern of inheritance and the rate of progression.
additionalDifferentials: Pigmentary retinopathy secondary to drug toxicity (e.g. phenothiazines), infection, or inflammation
additionalInvestigations: Electroretinography to demonstrate reduced or extinguished rod and later cone responses
Visual field testing to document peripheral constriction
Optical coherence tomography to assess the macula and detect cystoid macular oedema
Fundus autofluorescence imaging to map areas of degeneration
Genetic testing to identify the causative mutation and guide counselling and therapy
Systemic evaluation, including audiology, when a syndromic form is suspected
redFlags: Sudden or accelerated central visual loss suggesting macular oedema or another superimposed problem
Associated hearing loss indicating Usher syndrome requiring multidisciplinary care
Systemic features pointing to a syndromic association needing broader evaluation
New symptoms inconsistent with the expected slow progression, prompting search for another cause
reference.prognosis: Retinitis pigmentosa is generally slowly progressive, and although many patients retain useful central vision into adulthood, most eventually experience severe peripheral field loss; prognosis varies with genotype and inheritance pattern.
pitfalls: Overlooking treatable complications such as cystoid macular oedema and cataract that can improve vision
Failing to identify a syndromic association such as Usher or Bardet-Biedl syndrome
Not offering genetic counselling and testing to patients and at-risk relatives
Mistaking a pigmentary retinopathy from drug toxicity or prior inflammation for hereditary disease
management: Offer gene-replacement therapy with voretigene neparvovec for confirmed biallelic RPE65-mediated disease
Treat cystoid macular oedema with a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor such as oral acetazolamide or topical dorzolamide, and remove visually significant posterior subcapsular cataract surgically
Provide low-vision rehabilitation, visual aids, and ultraviolet-protective tinted lenses
Confirm the genotype with genetic testing to guide prognosis, counselling and eligibility for targeted therapy
Screen for and manage syndromic associations, including audiology for Usher syndrome and evaluation for Bardet-Biedl syndrome
Offer genetic counselling and family screening according to the inheritance pattern
Monitor with serial visual fields, optical coherence tomography and electroretinography, and consider emerging options such as retinal prostheses in advanced disease
